orders.explanation: Transcript 1 demonstrates broader and deeper technical competence: it traces the failure through schema editor logic and cross-backend introspection behavior, reproduces the bug cleanly, proposes the correct minimal fix (`unique=False` when deleting `index_together`), and validates the fix across multiple scenarios (including reverse-order removals) while referencing the likely upstream ticket and adding an appropriate inline comment. Transcript 2 finds the same fix but does so more mechanically, with several avoidable detours (encoding issues, SQLite schema editor in TestCase transaction) and less analysis of backend differences and migration implications.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it quickly pinpoints the failing code path, applies the minimal correct fix (filtering out unique constraints when deleting `index_together`), and then validates it with a direct reproduction plus running substantial portions of Django’s own test suite via `tests/runtests.py`. Transcript 2 also finds and applies the correct fix, but it spends significant time on unsuccessful/incorrect migration-state APIs (`render_migrations_state`, `ProjectState.render`, etc.) and doesn’t convincingly complete verification at the migration-operation level or with the test suite. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger execution reliability and end-to-end validation.

Transcript 1 is substantially more capable: it quickly locates the relevant upstream fix via `git log --grep`, applies a minimal, correct patch matching the known Django change, and validates it by temporarily applying and then reverting the upstream tests to keep the working tree clean. It also demonstrates strong debugging discipline (verifying failure without the fix, then re-running targeted suites) and avoids introducing unrelated modifications. Transcript 2 is much more ad hoc, introduces avoidable mistakes (calling a cached_property as a function, encoding issues), and ends by directly editing/adding tests in the repo without cleaning up, indicating weaker understanding of Django’s testing workflow and patch hygiene.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly located the exact upstream fix commit for the reported issue, applied a minimal and idiomatic patch that matches Django’s intended implementation, and validated it by running the relevant Django test runner with the appropriate labels. It also demonstrated strong repo/navigation skills (using `git log --grep`, `git show`, and clean diffs) and ensured only the necessary source change remained, avoiding test-patch conflicts. Transcript 1 eventually reached a working solution but made avoidable mistakes (treating a cached_property as callable, encoding issues, ad-hoc test edits) and was less precise and maintainable overall.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it pinpoints the exact root cause (AST defaults are right-aligned across `posonlyargs + args` and Sphinx wasn’t applying them to `posonlyargs` at all), demonstrates the bug with a targeted repro, derives the correct indexing logic from Python’s AST behavior, and validates across multiple edge cases plus end-to-end directive rendering and relevant test suites. It also distinguishes an unrelated pre-existing test failure from the change, showing stronger engineering judgment. Transcript 2 reaches a working fix, but the investigation and validation are less rigorous and the patch is less clearly justified/robustly checked.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it isolates the true root cause (AST default alignment across `posonlyargs + args.args`), implements a principled index calculation, and validates the fix against multiple edge cases and actual `inspect.signature` ground truth. It also runs relevant test suites and correctly identifies an unrelated, pre-existing autodoc failure by stashing changes to confirm. Transcript 1 reaches a working patch but is more meandering, includes a brittle string-replacement edit, and ends with an unresolved failing test without clearly diagnosing it as unrelated.

Transcript 1 shows a far more capable model: it iteratively debugs a full ARS implementation until it produces statistically correct samples across multiple distributions, implements the correct Gilks–Wild squeeze (chord-based lower hull), includes rigorous log-concavity/integrability checks that actively stop on violations, and builds a comprehensive modular test suite that consistently passes and writes the required sample files. Transcript 2 remains a partial/fragile implementation: it relies on truncated finite domains for tests, only warns (rather than reliably stopping) on non-log-concavity, has initialization and domain-handling limitations (e.g., cannot handle infinite bounds robustly), and its tests are comparatively weak and initially buggy. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper algorithmic correctness, robustness, and engineering discipline.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially higher capability: it implements a faithful Gilks & Wild ARS with correct upper-hull sampling, chord-based lower squeeze, and the crucial acceptance step, while handling infinite domains, numerical stability (log-space derivatives, near-parallel tangent intersections), and explicit integrability/log-concavity failure modes. It also supports function/call/expression densities, has a more comprehensive, interpretable test suite (including KS and non-log-concave rejection), and iteratively debugs subtle issues to convergence. Transcript 1 is comparatively fragile (finite-domain-centric, weaker/heuristic log-concavity handling, and less rigorous correctness guarantees), even though it eventually produces passing basic tests.

Transcript 1 shows stronger tool-use robustness and reasoning discipline: it compensates for missing `curl`/packages, correctly interprets the README’s “Science” mapping to biology/chemistry/physics, validates tokenizer behavior (special tokens) and even cross-checks concatenation effects before writing the final answer. Transcript 2 eventually arrives at the same token count, but includes substantial irrelevant content (a long graph-solution dump), more confusion around dataset metadata access, and less careful verification. Overall, Transcript 1 is more reliable and efficient in executing the requested workflow end-to-end.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it follows a clean, well-justified procedure: it reads the README, correctly maps “Science” to the dataset’s granular domains (physics/chemistry/biology), loads the proper `metadata` split, and verifies token-counting behavior with the Qwen2.5 tokenizer. It also performs extra consistency checks (source/domain alignment, concat-vs-sum token counts) and avoids the large irrelevant detour and structural confusion seen in Transcript 1. Overall it demonstrates better tooling adaptation, validation, and execution discipline.

Transcript 1 correctly diagnoses the crash as a lifetime/order interaction between the custom global new/delete heap and the patched libstdc++’s lazy locale facet registration/cleanup, and applies a minimal, standards-respecting fix by forcing facet registration in `user_init()` before the custom heap is enabled. It verifies the behavior with gdb/valgrind and preserves normal program termination semantics. Transcript 2 instead “fixes” the crash by calling `_exit(0)` to bypass all static destructors, which is a brittle workaround that changes shutdown behavior and can mask real leaks/cleanup requirements rather than resolving the underlying issue.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it identifies the precise root cause in the patched libstdc++ (lazy facet registration allocating via global `operator new` after the custom heap is enabled, then freed after the heap is destroyed) and applies a minimal, standards-respecting fix by forcing facet registration in `user_init()` before `g_custom_heap` becomes active. Transcript 1 “fixes” the crash by calling `_exit(0)` to bypass all static destructors, which is a blunt workaround that sidesteps normal teardown semantics and would generally be considered incorrect/fragile even if Valgrind shows no “lost” bytes. Transcript 2 also demonstrates stronger tool-driven validation and reasoning about initialization/teardown ordering.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly traces the regression via `git diff`, pinpoints the missing header control-character checks as a CWE-93 (CRLF injection) issue, and restores the original strict validation with informative `ValueError`s while keeping changes minimal and semantically aligned with upstream Bottle behavior. It also writes `/app/report.jsonl` using the expected CWE ID formatting (`"cwe-93"`), whereas Transcript 2 outputs `"CWE-93"` (different casing), which is likely to fail an “exact match” check in hidden evaluation. Transcript 1 demonstrates better diagnostic discipline and patch precision.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it correctly identified the vulnerability as a regression by inspecting `git diff`, connected it to the failing test, and restored the intended validation in `_hkey`/`_hval` with the appropriate `ValueError`. It also produced `report.jsonl` using the likely required CWE ID casing (`"cwe-93"`), matching the prompt’s example format, whereas Transcript 1 used `"CWE-93"` which may violate the “exact CWE-ids must appear” constraint. Despite a small manual-check slip, Transcript 2 corrected it quickly and verified all tests passed.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it handles real-world environment conflicts and test harness constraints robustly: it detects and resolves the pre-existing Nginx 8443 server-name conflict, uses a fast and safe `git archive`-based deployment, and crucially resets the bare repo and webroots to a pristine state to avoid branch-name collisions when the evaluator creates `main`/`dev`. Transcript 2 “works” in its own test, but leaves the remote with existing branches/commits (causing the harness’s `checkout -b main`/push flow to fail or require force), and its hook/NGINX choices are more brittle (e.g., branch detection via `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref "$refname"` in a bare hook). Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger debugging, operational correctness, and evaluator-aware setup.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it anticipates and resolves environment conflicts (the pre-existing Nginx default site already listening on 8443), then aligns deployments with the correct webroots and validates behavior end-to-end. Its `post-receive` hook uses `git archive | tar` (safer and faster than doing checkouts against a bare repo), handles branch deletions, and deploys full branch contents into stable directories with correct permissions. It also recognizes that leaving test branches in the remote could break the grader’s `checkout -b main/dev` flow and resets the repo/webroots to a pristine state, which Transcript 1 does not do.

Transcript 1 shows stronger troubleshooting and validation: it detects and fixes a protobuf field-numbering error, adapts to missing system utilities (`ps`, `ss`) by inspecting `/proc` and using a socket connectivity check, and verifies the server end-to-end with multiple RPC scenarios (including overwrite/persistence). Transcript 2 completes the basic setup but “verifies” server startup with a fallback message even when it can’t confirm the port is listening, and it risks starting duplicate servers (running `python server.py` twice) without handling bind errors. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates more robust execution and diagnostic skill.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it shows stronger robustness and debugging skill: it checks the environment, creates `/app` when missing, catches and fixes a proto schema error during code generation, and verifies the running server without relying on unavailable tools like `ps` by inspecting `/proc` and using `channel_ready_future` plus a socket reachability check. Transcript 1 completes the task, but its verification is weaker (it attempts `ps` and then falls back to a generic “started successfully” message) and it includes extra, non-required steps without as reliable process verification.

Transcript 2 converges on a simple, correct, and measurably faster implementation by swapping `numpy.linalg.eig` for `scipy.linalg.eig`, validating both correctness and speed across multiple runs and edge cases. Transcript 1 shows extensive low-level algorithm work with Numba/QR ideas, but it repeatedly encounters correctness, stability, and nondeterminism issues and never reaches a reliable faster-than-NumPy result within the transcript. The ability to identify a practical optimization that satisfies all constraints (accuracy, complex support, consistent speedup) makes Transcript 2 the more capable response here.

Transcript 1 converges on a simple, correct, and measurably faster implementation by switching to `scipy.linalg.eig`, and it validates both correctness (`np.allclose(A @ v, λv)`) and speed across repeated runs. Transcript 2 embarks on a much more complex custom QR/Schur + Numba approach, but it repeatedly encounters correctness issues, nondeterministic failures, heavy compile/import overhead, and ultimately demonstrates performance *worse* than NumPy for the target sizes—ending mid-debug without a stable, optimized solution. The ability to reach a robust, performant final implementation with appropriate verification makes Transcript 1 clearly more capable for this task.

Transcript 1 is more capable: it demonstrates a clear understanding of the cost model’s true degrees of freedom (batch S_max/G_max vs. declared shape), exploits this to minimize compile shapes (only 2 total), and uses an efficient dominance-constrained merging strategy to drive sequential_timecost down while keeping cost/pad/p95 within strict budgets. It also adds robustness by intentionally ordering batches to minimize the compile-latency hit and validates constraints/metrics comprehensively. Transcript 2 reaches a passing plan largely via trial-and-error parameter sweeps with many coding mistakes and much thinner margins (especially bucket 2 sequential_timecost), indicating weaker reasoning and execution discipline.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a deeper understanding of the evaluation function by exploiting the fact that the cost model derives \(S_{\max}\) and \(G_{\max}\) from the actual requests in a batch, not from the declared output “shape”, allowing it to use only 2 global shapes and minimize compile cost aggressively. It then applies a more sophisticated, constraint-aware greedy merge search to reduce sequential_timecost while tightly controlling cost, padding, and p95—achieving larger safety margins than Transcript 1. Transcript 1 reaches a valid solution, but its approach is more heuristic (fixed shape set + gen_len clustering) and lands closer to thresholds with less theoretical leverage.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger execution and troubleshooting: it generates the cert/key correctly (including a modern SAN), sets appropriate permissions on both the private key and the combined PEM, and performs multiple correctness checks (modulus match, self-verification). It also encounters a real Python parsing issue and methodically inspects the data structure, fixes the script, and removes a deprecation warning—showing better debugging and robustness. Transcript 2 eventually succeeds but has avoidable command/flow errors, leaves `server.pem` world-readable, and is overall less thorough in validation and hardening.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it demonstrates stronger debugging and validation behavior: it inspects the actual Python `ssl._test_decode_cert` subject structure after an error, fixes the parsing robustly, and then removes a deprecation warning. It also performs additional correctness checks (SAN for modern TLS compatibility, key/cert modulus match, `openssl verify`, explicit PEM block inspection) and applies stricter permissions to the combined PEM since it contains the private key. Transcript 1 completes the basic artifacts but has more trial-and-error around file creation and less comprehensive verification.

Transcript 1 is markedly more capable: it produces a robust, CPU-safe end-to-end pipeline that (a) actually uses MobileSAM correctly, (b) enforces single connected-component masks, (c) removes overlaps deterministically with a scalable owner-map approach, and (d) outputs valid non-rectangular polylines while preserving CSV structure (including handling index/no-index CSVs). It also anticipates real failure modes (weight key prefixes, contour simplification creating sliver overlaps, tiny/degenerate masks) and implements layered fallbacks with validation. Transcript 2 is comparatively naive—its “accumulated mask” overlap removal is order-dependent and can fragment/erase masks, it doesn’t rigorously enforce contiguity or non-rectangularity, and it relies on ad-hoc environment installs/downloads rather than a robust script suited for a hidden test setting.

Transcript 2 is clearly more capable: it develops a substantially more robust and scalable pipeline with careful model loading, prompt strategy tuning, CPU performance optimization (thread selection, embedding reuse), and extensive validation on both provided and synthetic edge-case datasets. It explicitly enforces the core constraints (single contiguous component, zero overlaps, non-rectangular polygon output) with dedicated post-processing and fallback logic, and it handles tricky CSV-format variations (with/without index column, header preservation) and weight key-prefix mismatches. Transcript 1 is a simpler “happy path” implementation that is slower, less robust, and does not convincingly guarantee the non-overlap/contiguity constraints across all cases.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it follows a cleaner, more standard build/install flow: it extracts the vendored source directly to `/app/sqlite`, builds with canonical `--coverage` flags, installs to `/usr/local/bin` (already on PATH) without brittle shell-profile hacks, and performs stronger verification (confirming `.gcda` generation and successfully running `gcov` on the correct `.gcno`). Transcript 2 works but is less robust: it nests the source under `/app/sqlite/sqlite`, installs into a custom prefix and then modifies `/etc/profile` to make PATH changes persist across sessions/tool calls, installs extra packages (tcl-dev/build-essential), and its `gcov sqlite3.gcno` check initially targets a non-executed unit (0% coverage).

Transcript 1 adheres more closely to the user’s constraints by building from the vendored tarball, configuring with explicit gcov flags, and installing SQLite under `/app/sqlite` (via `--prefix=/app/sqlite/install`) rather than diverting the install into `/usr/local`. It also performs stronger verification of instrumentation (e.g., `__gcov` symbols and presence of `.gcno/.gcda`) and then makes the installed binary available via PATH. Transcript 2 is competent but deviates from the “in /app/sqlite” intent by installing into `/usr/local` and additionally deletes coverage artifacts it just generated during verification.
